title: Additive Manufacturing (3D Printing)
summary: FDM, SLA, SLS and metal AM processes; design rules, orientation and anisotropy, tolerances, and when additive beats subtractive.

sections.heading: The Third Manufacturing Route
sections.content: Additive manufacturing (AM) builds parts **layer by layer** directly from CAD — no tools, no fixtures, no stock. Its promise is not "free complexity" (it is), but **economic freedom from geometry**: internal channels, lattices, topologically optimized shapes, and single-piece assemblies that any subtractive route would reject as impossible or uneconomic. AM is also the fastest route from CAD to physically real parts (see [[prototype-testing-and-validation|prototype]]), which is where most of industry's AM volume actually goes.

sections.heading: The AM Process Family
sections.content:
Choose the AM process by material and required quality:

| Process | Material | Tolerance / finish | Character |
|---|---|---|---|
| FDM (FFF) | PLA, ABS, PETG, nylon | ±0.2–0.5 mm, layered finish | Cheapest, structural-ish parts |
| SLA / DLP | Photopolymers | ±0.05–0.1 mm, smooth | Highest polymer detail (jewelry, dental) |
| SLS | Nylon powders | ±0.1–0.3 mm, no supports | Strong noneed-support polymer parts |
| SLM / DMLS | Steel, Al, Ti, Ni alloys | ±0.05–0.2 mm, rough surfaces | Production metal parts, lattices |
| MJF | Nylon | ±0.1–0.3 mm, fast | Production polymer at volume |
| DED | Metal wire/powder | ±0.5–1 mm | Large parts, repair, near-net |

Metal AM (SLM) is where "production additive" lives today: conformal cooling channels in injection mold inserts, orthopaedic implants, aerospace brackets — parts whose *internal geometry* pays for themselves. Polymer AM dominates prototypes, fixtures, and jigs.

sections.heading: Design Rules for Printing
sections.content:
Printability is a design discipline, not an afterthought:

- **Minimum feature**: ~0.4–0.8 mm for FDM walls, 0.1 mm for SLA/SLS; detail below the nozzle/laser resolution disappears.
- **Overhangs**: unsupported angles beyond ~45° (polymers) sag or need support; self-supported designs (45° chamfers, build-in-able features) save the support removal cost.
- **Holes** print round only when their axis is vertical; horizontal holes need teardrop profiles or support.
- **Lattices and gyroids** — the AM superpower: graded internal structure for stiffness/weight trade-offs; keep cell size ≥ 3–5× the wall resolution.
- **Internal channels** are free (the killer feature): conformal cooling channels, manifold passages — impossible to machine, printable in one piece.
- **Text/embossed detail**: minimum 0.5 mm text height per mm of depth; orientation matters (see next section).

sections.heading: Orientation & Anisotropy
sections.content:
Build orientation is the AM equivalent of grain direction:

- **Staircase roughness** on slanted faces: vertical faces are smoothest, slanted faces get the layer stair-step profile ($Ra \propto h/\cos\varphi$). Orient the cosmetic/critical surfaces vertical or near-vertical.
- **Anisotropy**: layer interfaces are the weak planes — tensile strength across layers is typically **70–85%** of in-plane (worse for FDM: ~50–60%; best for SLS/MJF). Load-bearing direction should lie **in-plane** with the layers.
- **Supports** hang below overhangs: orientation that minimizes supports lowers cost and removes surface scarring where supports touched.
- **Build time and cost** scale with **height** (layer count $n = H/h$) and machine footprint — orient for the smallest z-height when time matters.

Always ask the question in review: *which way will the load pull?* and set the build direction accordingly — it is the difference between a printed part that survives and one that delaminates in service.

sections.heading: Tolerances & Post-Processing
sections.content:
AM tolerances are honest about their limits:

- **As-printed**: ±0.1–0.3 mm typical (polymer), ±0.05–0.2 mm (metal) — **NOT** machining tolerance. Design fits and critical features accordingly, or plan post-machining.
- **Shrinkage/warp**: polymers shrink and curl (especially FDM large parts); metal parts need stress relief after build and can distort off the build plate.
- **Surface finish**: SLM surfaces are rough (Ra 3–12 µm) with adhered powder; polish, peen, or machine functional seal faces (see [[iso-fits-and-surface-finish|fits]] on why).
- **Post-processing ladder**: support removal → surface smoothing (vapor smoothing for nylon, tumbling, sanding) → stress relief/HIP for metal → CNC machining of datums and fits → coating.

Practical rule: **machine the functional features, print the rest** — a metal AM part with CNC-machined bearing seats and thread datums is the hybrid pattern that production actually uses.

sections.heading: When AM Wins (and Loses)
sections.content:
The economics, honestly stated:

**AM wins when:**
- Quantity is low (1–1000): no tooling to amortize — the break-even vs molding is far lower than most expect (see [[manufacturing-process-selection|process selection]]).
- Geometry is complex or **single-piece** (assemblies printed as one: elimination of joints, seals, fasteners).
- Internal features others cannot make (conformal cooling, lattices, serpentine channels).
- Lead time dominates: days of printing vs months of tooling for prototypes and spares.

**AM loses when:**
- Quantity is high with a stable design (molding/forging win by orders of magnitude in unit cost).
- Tolerances and finish are machining-grade across large surfaces.
- Material properties must match wrought specs exactly (fatigue of metal AM without HIP/post-processing is inferior — see [[fatigue-and-failure-analysis|fatigue]]).
- Cost per kilogram of raw material matters (powder is expensive).

The unit cost model is $C = c_t t + c_m m$ — machine time and material. AM competes on **avoided costs**: tooling, assembly, fixtures, inventory, and geometry-enabled performance — not on the raw cost sheet alone.

keyTakeaways: AM frees geometry (internal channels, lattices, single-piece assemblies) but prints anisotropically — orient the load in-plane.
Respect minimum features, 45° overhang rules, and orientation-driven staircase roughness.
As-printed tolerances are ±0.1–0.3 mm, not machining grade — machine the functional features.
AM wins at low volume and high complexity; molding/forging win at high volume. Cost = ct·t + cm·m.
